one_liner: NASA JPL's no_std Wasm 1.0 interpreter for flight software; compiles plus instantiates modules about 60x faster than Wasmtime or Wasmer Cranelift.
what_it_does: A Rust no_std decoder, validator and interpreter for WebAssembly 1.0 (MVP plus mutable globals and custom page sizes), built to run command sequences and low-trust code on spacecraft. The embedder creates an Engine with fixed-capacity host modules, streams the binary in chunks through a WasmStream into Module::new (which decodes, validates and translates in one pass into IR pages held by a CodeBuilder), then drives Interpreter.run with an instruction budget. Its API differs from Wasmtime's and Wasmer's. A C API crate (spacewasm_c_api) and a WASI 0.1 command-line runner (spacewasi) are included.
how_it_is_fast: Startup is cheap because there is no optimizing back end. A single streaming pass decodes, validates and lowers the bytecode into a fixed-width IR of 16-bit words, with indexes and branch targets already resolved. No machine code is generated and nothing gets a second pass. Execution is a plain stack-machine interpreter (a visitor dispatching one IR instruction at a time, counting fuel per instruction), so the startup advantage over JITs disappears on long runs.
when_to_use: Embedded or no_std Rust hosts that must load a module from flash or a file in chunks, without holding the whole binary in one contiguous buffer.
Systems with flight-software memory rules: allocation only during module initialisation, from a capped set of fixed-size pages, with failures returned as errors and never panics.

Hosts that need bounded, resumable execution: run() takes an instruction budget and returns OutOfFuel, host functions can pause the engine and resume it later, and interpreted calls do not use the native stack.
Short-lived invocations of MVP modules where compile plus instantiate time dominates: about 0.1 ms for CoreMark or an ERC-20 contract on an EPYC 7763, against about 10 ms for Wasmtime (Cranelift).
when_not_to_use: Compute-heavy or long-running code: its execution geomean in the same suite is x79.53 of the fastest, against WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07 and Wasmtime Pulley x27.92, and JITs are far faster.

Modules that use post-MVP features (bulk memory, sign extension, non-trapping float-to-int, multi-value, SIMD, tail calls). Recent clang and rustc emit some of these by default, so you have to build with -mcpu=mvp or post-process with the bundled wasm2mvp.sh.

When only the lowest startup matters: Wasmi v2 lazy (x1.37), wasm3 lazy, DLR-FT wasm-interpreter, submilli-wasm and toywasm all start faster, and V8 starts faster on the three largest modules (spidermonkey 10.9 ms vs 65.2 ms, ffmpeg 35.5 ms vs 293.0 ms).
Untrusted modules on 32-bit targets, or modules with more than 65,535 functions or globals, until open issues #158 and #201 are fixed.

Projects that need a stable API: 13 crates.io releases between 0.4.4 (2026-07-27) and 0.7.1 (2026-09-04), and CompilerOptions changed between the 0.5.2 API used by the benchmark adapter and the repo's own HEAD bench.

integration.form: crate (no_std); also a C static/shared library via crates/spacewasm_c_api
integration.dependencies: libm =0.2.16 only (pinned under the project's no-dependencies requirement); the embedder must install an allocator through the spacewasm::global_allocator! macro (its own C-ABI hooks, not Rust's #[global_allocator])
integration.platforms: any Rust no_std target in principle; uses x86 inline asm (sqrtss) for some float ops, with a miri-soft-floats feature to switch to soft floats; 32-bit targets have an open decoder-panic bug (#158)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; an Engine owns one interpreter stack and run() takes &mut Engine, so use one engine per thread

gotchas: Open issue #201 (2026-09-14): get_func_ref and get_global_ref narrow a validated index with 'as u16'. A module with 65,537 globals validates, and global.get 65536 silently returns global 0's value. Issue #158: a malformed module panics the decoder on 32-bit targets, which contradicts the no-panic requirement on the flight targets it aims at.

Benchmark harness asymmetries (from wasmi-benchmarks source, effect on the numbers not measured). The SpaceWasm adapter replaces the flight PageAllocator with plain malloc/free and feeds the module in copied 1 KiB chunks. The Wasmtime adapter builds wasmtime 47.0.3 with default-features = false (runtime and anyhow only), so the default parallel-compilation feature is off: Cargo.lock shows no rayon under wasmtime, while the Wasmer compilers do pull rayon. The 63x gap to stock Wasmtime Cranelift on a multi-core machine is therefore likely overstated, though Wasmer (Cranelift), whose compilers pull rayon, was only about 10% faster than Wasmtime (Cranelift) here.

Only startup was measured in its favour: the comparison is a single-pass interpreter translator against optimizing JITs. Among eager translators doing the same full validation and translation, SpaceWasm beats Wasmi v2 eager and wasm3 eager on 6 of 7 modules but loses on pulldown-cmark (8.8 ms vs 5.3 ms and 8.1 ms) (derived from page data).

The IR is fixed-width and usually larger than the bytecode. Hard limits include 256 modules per store, 255 parameter words, 65,535 local words, 32-byte import and custom-section names, and a ±2,097,151-instruction branch range; a longer import name is rejected at decode time. unsafe code sits in the stack, memory and IR-reader hot paths and relies on the up-front validator; the strict-assertions feature re-checks bounds at run time.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick SpaceWasm over Wasmi or wasm3 when its flight-software constraints matter more than speed: no_std, init-only fixed-page allocation, chunked streaming decode and fuel-bounded resumable execution. Wasmi starts and executes faster. Pick it over DLR-FT wasm-interpreter, which starts faster (x10.95 vs x25.84) and whose requirement set SpaceWasm adopted, if you want NASA JPL's implementation with its C API and WASI runner.
verified_claims_summary: In the third-party wasmi-benchmarks startup suite (time to compile, validate and instantiate 7 modules from a 0.1 ms ERC-20 contract to ffmpeg; criterion; bench profile with fat LTO; AMD EPYC 7763, probably a GitHub Actions VM; spacewasm 0.5.2, wasmtime 47.0.3, wasmer 7.2.1), SpaceWasm's geomean is x25.84 of the per-case fastest, against x1634.19 for Wasmtime (Cranelift) and x1484.15 for Wasmer (Cranelift). That is about 63x and 57x faster startup; per case, CoreMark takes 0.109 ms vs 9.87 ms and ffmpeg 0.293 s vs 17.96 s against Wasmtime (Cranelift). The rustc version and suite commit are not recorded.
status_note: Active and Apache-2.0 (1.6k stars, last commit 2026-09-28, frequent 0.x releases with API churn). Usable as a crate today for MVP modules, but test and validator coverage is still being fixed: open issue #209 says the README overstates unit-test instruction coverage, and #206 says the differential validator oracle tests never run in CI.
